opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that so much of the world now runs on software, and a lot of that software is old, sprawling, and maintained by fewer people than you'd hope. When you think about banking systems, hospitals, power grids, open-source libraries that sit underneath basically everything, the code is often written by people who've long since moved on, and the knowledge of why it works the way it does has kind of evaporated.

So understanding code is actually the bottleneck in a lot of cases, more than writing it. Most engineers spend the majority of their time reading, trying to build a mental model of a system before they dare touch it. And review is where we catch the mistakes that matter: the subtle bug, the security hole, the change that looks fine in isolation but breaks an assumption three files away.

What's exciting now is that models have gotten good enough to really help there. They can read a large codebase tirelessly, trace through how things connect, and flag issues a human reviewer might miss at the end of a long day. And as we're generating more code with AI, the volume goes up, so the ability to review and verify has to scale with it. Otherwise you're just producing more surface area for problems.

For me, it's really about trust. If we want software to be something society can rely on, we need tools that help people understand what's actually running and catch problems before they ship. Making that kind of rigor cheap and accessible, not just something the biggest companies can afford, I think is one of the most meaningful things we can do.

r001.rationale: The response describes understanding code written by former maintainers and review as a way to catch mistakes, but does not clearly frame code review as helping people understand that code.

r002.rationale: It mentions catching security holes, but does not assert that many software vulnerabilities remain undiscovered.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we're at a point where the amount of code being written is about to massively outpace the amount of code that anyone can actually read. With agents like Codex, you can generate a pull request in minutes that would have taken an engineer a day. That's incredible for productivity, but it changes where the bottleneck is. The bottleneck is no longer writing the code, it's understanding it, trusting it, and knowing whether it actually does what you intended.

And when you look at the software that society really depends on, the stuff running in hospitals, in banks, in power grids, in the systems that route your flight or process your paycheck, a lot of that code is old, poorly documented, and understood by very few people. In some cases the people who understood it have retired. So there's already a comprehension debt in the world, and if we just pile more generated code on top of it without better tools for reviewing and understanding, we make that debt worse, not better.

So I see review and code understanding tools as the thing that keeps us honest. A good reviewer doesn't just check for syntax errors, it asks: what are the assumptions here, what breaks if this input is wrong, does this change the behavior of something three modules away that nobody is thinking about. If we can get models to do that kind of reasoning well, at scale, and surface it to humans in a way that is clear, then we actually raise the floor on software quality across the board, including for the small team maintaining some critical system that never had the budget for a dedicated security review.

The other piece is that trust has to be earned incrementally. We're not going to get to a world where people hand over critical infrastructure to agents in one step, nor should we. The way you get there is by having tools that make the agent's work legible, where you can see why it made a change, what it tested, what it was unsure about. Review is the interface between human judgment and machine output. If that interface is good, we can move fast and stay safe. If it's bad, we end up either moving slowly because nobody trusts anything, or moving fast and breaking things that really shouldn't break.

r001.rationale: The response presents review as helping people understand and assess code produced by agents, making that work legible to human reviewers.

r002.rationale: It mentions security review and possible failures, but does not assert that many software vulnerabilities remain undiscovered.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of society runs on software that no single person fully understands. And when we need to change that software, the hard part is often understanding why it was built a certain way, what depends on it, and what might break.

Tools that help us understand and review code can make those changes easier to reason about. They can help people find problems, question assumptions, and check whether a change actually does what was intended. That matters especially for systems people depend on, where a small mistake can have consequences far beyond the code itself.

And as we get better at generating code, we need to get better at reviewing it too. Writing more software is only useful if we can maintain it and have good reasons to trust it.

r001.rationale: The response says code can be hard to understand and that review tools help, but it does not clearly connect this to understanding code written by someone else.

r002.rationale: The response mentions finding problems and avoiding mistakes, but does not assert that many software vulnerabilities remain undiscovered.

sol-6.1.text:
Software underpins so much of our lives, and our ability to trust it depends on our ability to understand what it does. A small change can have consequences far beyond the lines of code being edited, and those consequences are often hard to see in a large system.

That’s why tools for understanding and reviewing code matter. They can help people trace how a system works, question assumptions, and catch mistakes before they affect users. And as AI makes it easier to produce more code, that ability to review and verify it becomes even more important. Writing code is only part of the job; we also need to make sure people can confidently maintain the systems we depend on.

r001.rationale: The response says code review helps people trace how a system works, but does not specify that the code was written by someone else.

r002.rationale: It mentions catching mistakes, but does not assert that many software vulnerabilities remain undiscovered.
